spots.name: Capilano Suspension Bridge
spots.label: Capilano Bridge

text.geographic_location: In Upper Capilano, in the District of North Vancouver, inside Capilano Suspension Bridge Park on the Capilano River canyon.
text.description:
The Capilano Suspension Bridge is a simple suspension bridge across the Capilano River in the District of North Vancouver. It is about 140 metres long and 70 metres above the water, so it photographs well: a thin line of deck hanging over a deep canyon, with dark forest on both sides. The first bridge was built in 1889 by George Grant Mackay, using hemp ropes and cedar planks. The present bridge dates from a complete rebuild in 1956. It belongs to a private park that draws over 1.2 million visitors a year, so expect company on the span itself.

For a picture of the whole bridge rather than a view along it, use the Cliffwalk. This attraction was added to the park in June 2011, and its designated photo platforms along the cliff face let you frame the full bridge with the river and trees below for scale. Photo-stop signs mark where to pause. Take your shots at those marked spots and stay behind the railings. If the Cliffwalk is busy, the Nature's Edge Boardwalk is a good alternative: it shows the bridge through the rainforest trees, away from the crowds on the span.

The bridge sways when it is full of people, so pictures taken from on it can come out blurred. Taking the wide shot from the platforms avoids that.
text.directions_text: No SkyTrain or other rail stop is close, so check the official site or a journey planner for the way to Capilano Suspension Bridge Park (3735 Capilano Road, North Vancouver). Once inside the park, head for the Cliffwalk, near the bridge end. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.access_note: This is a private, ticketed park, so all the photo spots described here are inside paid entry; check the official site before you go.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the bridge deck along the lower third line, so the trees and river fill the rest. Keep the railing out of the corners of the frame, and wait for gaps in the crowd on the span. For a quieter, more natural view, the Nature's Edge Boardwalk shows the bridge through the forest trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time of day when the park is quieter, as fewer people on the span give a cleaner picture. Soft, even light on a bright overcast day also works well under the trees. Check the official site before you go for current hours and the winter Canyon Lights times.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (designated photo platforms along the cliff face, near the bridge end). The whole suspension bridge spanning the canyon, with the river and trees below for scale. From here the whole suspension bridge spans the canyon, with the river and trees below to show how high it is.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the whole bridge across the canyon in one frame. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the platform is crowded and you need to fit more in. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the span and the walkers on it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the deck and trees keep their detail. Take a few frames, as the bridge moves when busy. In winter, if you stay for the Canyon Lights display, use night mode and hold the phone as still as you can against a rail or your body.

spots.alt: Capilano Suspension Bridge, Vancouver: a simple suspension bridge across the Capilano River. Photo spot

spots.name: Gastown and the Steam Clock
spots.label: Gastown

text.geographic_location: In Gastown, in the north-west part of the Downtown Eastside next to Downtown Vancouver, at the corner of Water Street and Cambie Street, just back from the Burrard Inlet waterfront.
text.description:
Gastown is Vancouver's oldest neighbourhood, named after "Gassy" Jack Deighton, a Yorkshire seaman who opened a saloon here in 1867. Its best-known photo subject is the steam clock on the corner of Water and Cambie Streets. The clock was built in 1977 over a steam grate, and it runs on steam from the downtown heating network. Steam also sounds its whistles, which play a Westminster-style chime. It has four faces, a domed top and, on a cold day, plumes of steam, with the brick heritage buildings of Water Street behind. That mix of old brick and a quirky machine is why it photographs so well. Gastown became a National Historic Site of Canada in 2009. The clock itself is a modern invention, though it is promoted as a heritage feature.

Arrive three or four minutes before a quarter hour to catch the whistle and the steam. Crowds gather, especially at the top of the hour and at midday in summer, so be patient and keep out of the walking path. If you have time, Maple Tree Square and the narrow Blood Alley are worth a few more frames, particularly after dark when the lamps are lit.
text.directions_text: Take the SkyTrain Expo Line or Canada Line to Waterfront station, then head south-east; it is about 3 minutes on foot. Alternatively, use Granville station on the SkyTrain Expo Line and walk north-east, about 6 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.access_note: The clock stands on an open public street corner, in an area that is now pedestrian-friendly; check the official site before you go for any street changes or events.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the clock upright in the centre or just off to one side, leaving space above the dome for the steam. For an alternative, try Maple Tree Square with its Victorian brick corners and a view down Carrall Street. The Gassy Jack statue is no longer there to frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Arrive 3-4 minutes before a quarter hour for the whistle. The steam shows best on cold days, from late autumn to March. Crowds gather especially at the top of the hour and at midday in summer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Water Street and Cambie Street (south side of Water Street, facing the clock). The full clock with its domed top and steam plumes, set against the brick heritage buildings of Water Street behind it. From here the full clock with its domed top and steam plumes sits against the brick heritage buildings behind it. Stay out of the pedestrian walking path while you shoot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole clock with the brick buildings behind it. Switch to 2x or 3x telephoto if you want the dome and steam without the crowd around the base.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the clock to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the steam stays white and the sky does not wash out. Turn on Live Photos or motion to catch the steam moving. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a wall.

spots.alt: Gastown and the Steam Clock, Vancouver: Vancouver's oldest neighbourhood. Photo spot

spots.name: Stanley Park and the Seawall
spots.label: Stanley Park

text.geographic_location: Stanley Park covers the north-western end of Vancouver's downtown peninsula, beside the West End and Coal Harbour neighbourhoods. Prospect Point is at the park's northern tip, right above the Lions Gate Bridge.
text.description: Stanley Park is a 405-hectare public park that fills the north-western half of Vancouver's downtown peninsula, with Burrard Inlet on one side and English Bay on the other. For photos it works as a set of different views rather than one picture: dark forest, rocky shoreline, beaches, and the long Seawall that runs around the edge. Opened in September 1888, it was Vancouver's first park. Much of it is still thick forest, with about half a million trees, some as tall as 76 metres. Guides call it the park's signature lookout. From here you look down on the Lions Gate Bridge, with Burrard Inlet, the North Shore mountains and the forest edge behind it. If you have time to walk on, two other pictures are worth a try. Brockton Point Lighthouse, the park's easternmost point, has totem poles beside it and the harbour behind. Siwash Rock is a lone sea stack with one tree on top, near Third Beach. In the viewpoint photos, keep the bridge and the mountains as your main subjects and let the trees frame one side. The Seawall is busy in summer, so shoot quickly and step out of the way of walkers and cyclists.
text.directions_text: The nearest SkyTrain station on the map is Burrard (SkyTrain Expo Line), about 2.2 km (roughly half an hour on foot) from Stanley Park. Prospect Point is about 1.6 km further north through the park. If you would rather not walk that far, take a taxi to Prospect Point. The nearest ferry stop is Maritime Museum Dock (False Creek Ferries), about 2.4 km from the park. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.access_note: Stanley Park is an open public park, but check the official site before you go for any path or Seawall closures.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the bridge deck along a lower third line, so the mountains fill the upper part of the frame. Include a strip of dark treetop in one corner to give depth. If you walk on, Brockton Point Lighthouse and its totem poles make a good second picture, and Siwash Rock makes a good third from the Seawall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk, when the bridge lights come on against the fading sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Prospect Point (northern tip of Stanley Park, lookout above the Lions Gate Bridge). The Lions Gate Bridge framed against the Burrard Inlet, the North Shore mountains and the forest edge. From here the bridge sits against Burrard Inlet, with the North Shore mountains and the forest edge behind it. This is the clearest place in the park for the bridge with mountains behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene of bridge, inlet and mountains. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the bridge towers or the far mountain ridges. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the forest and shoreline at the lighthouse or Siwash Rock.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bridge to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. When the bridge lights come on at dusk, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body or a solid surface for a few seconds. On the Seawall the inner lane is for pedestrians and bikes go one way only, so step aside before you stop to shoot.

spots.alt: Stanley Park and the Seawall, Vancouver: a 405-hectare public park. Photo spot
